content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with the planners and presenters of this report, have disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. However, two exceptions exist: Jeffrey P. Salomone, who has received an honorarium as a consultant and member of the Advisory Board for Schering-Plough Pharmaceuticals, and Stewart C. Wang, who has received research grants from General Motors and Toyota Motors while serving as a principal investigator for these grants. At the scene of any traumatic injury, emergency medical services (EMS) providers must identify patients at the highest risk for severe injury and determine the most appropriate facility for transport based on the type and severity of injuries. This process, known as field triage, relies on a decision-making algorithm called a decision scheme. The first Field Triage Decision Scheme was published by the American College of Surgeons (ACS) in 1986, with updates in 1990, 1993, and 1999. In 2005, the CDC, supported by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), began revising the scheme by convening the National Expert Panel on Field Triage, which included injury-care providers, public health professionals, automotive industry representatives, and federal agency officials. The most recent revision, published in 2006 by the ACS Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), introduced changes to the triage criteria, including additions, modifications, and removals of certain criteria. The 2006 version of the Field Triage Decision Scheme reflects significant updates from the 1999 version. These changes include the addition of new criteria, modifications to existing criteria, and the removal of outdated criteria. The recommendations in this report have been endorsed by numerous organizations, including the American College of Surgeons, the American College of Emergency Physicians, and the National Association of EMS Physicians, among others. The NHTSA has also concurred with the contents of this report. Injuries are a major global public health issue, accounting for approximately 5 million deaths annually, or about 10% of all deaths worldwide. Millions more are disabled temporarily or permanently each year due to injuries, imposing a substantial burden on families, communities, and societies. The global burden of injury is expected to rise significantly by 2020. In the United States, injuries are the leading cause of death for individuals aged 1–44 years. In 2005, injuries accounted for approximately 174,000 deaths and 41 million emergency department visits. The economic cost of injuries is also substantial, with billions of dollars spent annually on medical care and lost productivity. The optimal approach to reducing the morbidity, mortality, and economic consequences of injuries is prevention. However, when prevention fails, EMS providers must ensure that patients receive prompt and appropriate emergency care at the scene and are transported to the most suitable healthcare facility for further evaluation and treatment. The choice of facility can significantly impact patient outcomes, as trauma centers have specialized expertise and resources for treating severely injured patients. Trauma centers are classified into levels (I–IV) based on the scope of resources and services available, with Level I centers providing the highest level of care. Not all injured patients require transport to a Level I trauma center. Patients with less severe injuries may be better served by transport to a closer emergency department. Overburdening Level I trauma centers with all injured patients, regardless of injury severity, could reduce their availability for the most critically injured patients. Studies have shown that severely injured patients treated at Level I trauma centers have a 25% reduction in mortality compared to those treated at non-trauma centers. The development of field triage criteria has paralleled the evolution of trauma centers. The initial 1976 guidance by ACS-COT included physiologic and anatomic measures for stratifying patients by injury severity but did not specify triage criteria. Subsequent studies demonstrated reduced mortality in regions with specialized trauma centers, leading to the publication of the first ACS field triage protocols in 1986. These protocols have since served as the basis for field triage in most EMS systems in the United States, with local adaptations to reflect specific operational contexts. Trauma centers are acute-care facilities that meet specific resource and personnel standards to provide care for severely injured patients. They ensure 24-hour access to surgeons, anesthesiologists, and other specialists, as well as resuscitation and life-support equipment. Trauma centers are designated as Level I, II, III, or IV based on their resources and capabilities. Level I centers provide comprehensive care, including prevention, rehabilitation, education, and research, while Level IV centers focus on initial stabilization and transfer to higher-level facilities if needed. Trauma systems are part of a broader public health framework that conceptualizes traumatic injury as a disease involving interactions among the host, agent, and environment. This framework emphasizes prevention, mitigation of injury effects, and continuous improvement of the trauma system. Inclusive trauma systems integrate all acute healthcare facilities, allowing for a tiered approach to trauma care, while exclusive systems focus solely on specialized trauma centers. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of inclusive trauma systems in improving patient outcomes and reducing mortality. The accuracy of field triage is critical for matching the severity of a patient's injuries with the appropriate level of care. Various standardized systems, such as the Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) and the Injury Severity Score (ISS), have been developed to classify injuries by type and severity. These systems allow for comparisons of medical outcomes across different treatment regimens and have been used to predict mortality and other outcomes in trauma research. For example, patients with an ISS greater than 15 are considered to have severe injuries and are at higher risk for mortality and complications.
